edition: Director's cut pilot / editorial preview / 17 October 2026
title: Making Medicines Keep
story_question: How could a customer in thirteenth-century Cairo judge whether a prepared medicine would remain dependable?
scientific_status: Historical interpretation; archival comparison images are NOT the Cairo manuscript itself.
source: Making Medicines Keep: Syrups, Substitution, and Pharmaceutical Reliability in Ayyubid-Mamluk Cairo; accepted by History of Pharmacy and Pharmaceuticals on 15 October 2026.
narrator: kokoro-onnx / male and female audition exports; not author voice, never voice-cloned
music: Original room tone and restrained non-melodramatic drone; keep consonants clear and leave the opening nearly silent.

chapters.title: After the fire
chapters.narration: A syrup can look ready when it leaves the fire. Tomorrow it may crystallize or change consistency. The person buying it cannot watch what happened in the shop.

shots.credit: Original editorial depiction of syrup failure; not an artifact
Original interpretive illustration of crystallization; not a measurement

chapters.title: The city and the shop
chapters.narration: The problem leads us to medieval Cairo, where medicinal preparation belonged to daily trade. Recipes and judgments about workmanship entered the same written record.

shots.credit: Qalawun complex, present-day photograph, Wikimedia Commons CC BY 4.0; architecture, not period footage
Original editorial reconstruction, not a photographed medieval shop

chapters.title: A base called julab
chapters.narration: The pharmacy manual Minhaj al-dukkan begins its discussion of syrups with julab, made from sugar and rose water. The ingredients are named, but making them behave takes work.

shots.credit: Walters Art Museum, Arabic Dioscorides manuscript made in Baghdad, 1224, CC0; NOT an illustration of Cairo or of Minhaj al-dukkan
Illustration of a sugar and rose-water base; not a documentary vessel

chapters.title: The endpoint is not a number
chapters.narration: Heat. Remove the foam. Strain. Then judge the qiwam, the achieved consistency. It was a practical decision made at the vessel, not a numerical reading from an instrument.

shots.credit: Reconstructed preparation sequence, not a record of a historical experiment
Syrup consistency interpretation; no quantitative viscosity values are implied

chapters.title: Instructions for what went wrong
chapters.narration: The manual even considers preparations that do not turn out as expected. Its advice is revealing: pharmaceutical knowledge included recognizing failure and deciding what might be repaired.

shots.credit: Original illustration of crystallization; symbolic, not sampled material
Metropolitan Museum of Art, Baghdad-school Dioscorides leaf, 1224, public domain; contextual rather than a source for Cairo text

chapters.title: A different surviving voice
chapters.narration: A Cairo Genizah prescription offers another kind of evidence: powdered ingredients kneaded with rose syrup. It records an instruction, not proof that every dose was made as written.

shots.credit: Typeset interpretation of Cambridge Genizah Or.1081 J39; original leaf not reproduced
Original editorial illustration; not a Cairo Genizah scan

chapters.title: Substitution has rules
chapters.narration: If an ingredient was unavailable, substitution could be discussed openly. That is different from hiding a cheaper ingredient. Market-oversight writings asked how deception could be detected.

shots.credit: Conceptual explanation of historically discussed substitution; NOT modern bioequivalence
Interpretation of market oversight; not evidence of inspections at one named shop

chapters.title: What could be relied upon?
chapters.narration: The question behind my article is what counted as dependable medicine under those conditions. Not modern quality control in disguise, but a historically specific craft with its own limits.

shots.credit: Original film title card; article accepted 15 October 2026, not yet labelled published
Author's contemporary portrait; not a historical manuscript
